title: A Cancer Vaccine Made for One Patient? Hyderabad's RNA Foundry Is Building It
excerpt: PopVax's RNA Foundry aims to design personalised mRNA cancer vaccines from a patient's own tumour, at an estimated $300,000 and eight to ten weeks per vaccine — still experimental, and not yet given to any patient.
body:
• Hyderabad-based PopVax launched its RNA Foundry in October 2026, a research, development and manufacturing facility for personalised mRNA cancer vaccines built from an individual patient's tumour mutations.
  • PopVax says it is committing to making more than 100 personalised cancer vaccines in the next 12 months, on a case-by-case basis.
  • The estimated cost of designing and manufacturing one such vaccine is around $300,000, or approximately Rs 2.5 crore, with a typical timeframe of eight to ten weeks.
  • These vaccines are experimental and have not yet been administered to patients — there is no clinical efficacy data for PopVax's candidates, and they are not a substitute for established cancer treatment.

A cancer vaccine designed for one patient, and no one else, is what a Hyderabad biotechnology company says it can now build. PopVax, founded in 2021, unveiled its RNA Foundry in October 2026 — a full-stack research, development and manufacturing facility that aims to deliver personalised cancer vaccines, according to the company's announcement reported by Global News 365 and examined by India Today / The CSR Journal.

How a vaccine for one patient works

Most cancer vaccines in development by large pharmaceutical companies are standardised for broader populations. A personalised vaccine starts instead from the mutations in one person's tumour. Those genetic changes can produce abnormal proteins called neoantigens, which mark cancer cells as different from healthy ones. Scientists design an mRNA sequence instructing the body's cells to produce selected tumour targets, training the immune system — particularly T-cells — to recognise and attack cells displaying them. Identifying a target, however, does not guarantee the immune system will eradicate the cancer, a caution Dr Rahul Thakur, a consultant radiation oncologist at TGH ONCO LIFE Cancer Centre, raised in the India Today report.

What PopVax says the Foundry will do

PopVax said the facility uses its proprietary mRNA platform and a fridge-stable lipid nanoparticle formulation, and is built to align with global Good Manufacturing Practices. The company said it is committing to making more than 100 personalised cancer vaccines in the next 12 months, and is asking people to email their cancer type and stage and sequencing details so vaccines can be developed on a case-by-case basis. Founder Soham Sankaran announced the launch on social media, noting that making high-quality mRNA medicine was not an easy task.

The price, the wait, and the evidence gap

The figures attached to the offer are steep and the status is early. The estimated cost for designing and manufacturing such a vaccine is around $300,000, or approximately Rs 2.5 crore, with a typical timeframe of eight to ten weeks. The vaccines are still in the experimental stage and have not yet been administered to patients, so there is no efficacy data for PopVax's own candidates.

The wider field offers encouragement, not proof. A Moderna and Merck collaboration on a personalised mRNA vaccine, intismeran autogene, with pembrolizumab (Keytruda) for high-risk melanoma reported a two-year recurrence-free survival rate of 82.2% for the combination against 70% for pembrolizumab alone in 2026 trial results — findings that, as the India Today report notes, pertain to a specific cancer type and patient group and cannot be generalised to all personalised vaccines.

What patients should take from this

For diaspora families weighing treatment options in India, the practical reading is narrow: a manufacturing capability now exists in Hyderabad, at a stated price and timeline, for an experimental product. Experts quoted in the reporting advise that such vaccines should not replace established therapies, that cancer type, stage and existing options should be evaluated first with an oncologist, and that possible side effects include fever, fatigue and injection-site reactions. The next evidence to watch is whether any PopVax-made vaccine is administered, and under what clinical protocol.
